title: Conjecture on polynomial-time solvability of bounded sub-determinant integer programs
statement_text: Integer programs with bounded sub-determinants can be solved in polynomial time. In particular, the stable set problem on graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G) \leq k$ is polynomial for every fixed $k$.
context_text: An integer program has bounded sub-determinants if its (integer) constraint matrix $A$ has all square submatrices with determinant bounded in absolute value by a fixed constant $\Delta$; the belief is that for every fixed $\Delta$ such programs $\max\{w^\top x: Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}$ can be solved in polynomial time (for $\Delta=1$, totally unimodular matrices, this is linear programming). The odd cycle packing number $\mathrm{ocp}(G)$ is the maximum number of vertex-disjoint odd cycles in $G$. The stable set problem asks for a maximum-weight stable (independent) set for given vertex weights $w$; it can be written as the integer program $\max\{w^\top x: Mx\le\mathbf{1},\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V(G)}\}$, where $M$ is the edge-vertex incidence matrix of $G$, and the largest absolute value of a determinant of a square submatrix of $M$ is $2^{\mathrm{ocp}(G)}$. Exact polynomial-time algorithms were known only for $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=0$ (bipartite graphs) and $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=1$ (Artmann, Weismantel and Zenklusen, who solve integer programs whose constraint matrix has all sub-determinants bounded by 2 in absolute value, in strongly polynomial time); for bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ a PTAS is known. The authors note that recent work links the complexity of integer programs to the magnitude of their sub-determinants, making the belief tempting; it would imply that stable set is polynomial for every fixed bound $k$ on $\mathrm{ocp}(G)$, which remains open for $k\ge2$. The paper proves this consequence for graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G)\le k$ embedded in a surface of Euler genus at most $g$, for fixed $k$ and $g$.
notes: Stated as 'it is tempting to believe'; the paper explicitly confirms the problem is open for $k \geq 2$. No labelled theorem environment.

title: Open question on stable set for bounded ocp and arbitrary Euler genus
statement_text: Is the stable set problem polynomial-time solvable for graphs $G$ with $\mathrm{ocp}(G) \leq k$ (for fixed $k$) embedded in a surface of arbitrary Euler genus?
context_text: The odd cycle packing number $\mathrm{ocp}(G)$ is the maximum number of vertex-disjoint odd cycles in $G$. The stable set problem asks for a maximum-weight stable (independent) set for given vertex weights $w$; it can be written as the integer program $\max\{w^\top x: Mx\le\mathbf{1},\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V(G)}\}$, where $M$ is the edge-vertex incidence matrix of $G$, and the largest absolute value of a determinant of a square submatrix of $M$ is $2^{\mathrm{ocp}(G)}$. Exact polynomial-time algorithms were known only for $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=0$ (bipartite graphs) and $\mathrm{ocp}(G)=1$ (Artmann, Weismantel and Zenklusen, who solve integer programs whose constraint matrix has all sub-determinants bounded by 2 in absolute value, in strongly polynomial time); for bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ a PTAS is known. The Euler genus of a surface obtained from the sphere by adding $h$ handles and $c$ crosscaps is $2h+c$; surfaces may be non-orientable. The paper's main result is a polynomial-time algorithm for maximum-weight stable set in graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G)\le k$ embedded in a (possibly non-orientable) surface of Euler genus at most $g$, for fixed $k$ and $g$, together with a polynomial-size extended formulation of the stable set polytope. Without a bound on $\mathrm{ocp}$ the problem is NP-hard already for planar graphs. The natural examples of graphs with bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ come from embeddings in non-orientable surfaces of Euler genus $k$ in which every odd cycle is one-sided (Lovász's characterization of graphs with no two disjoint odd cycles). The authors do not know whether the genus bound can be dropped, i.e. whether only the bound on $\mathrm{ocp}$ suffices; a positive answer for all graphs would follow from polynomial solvability of bounded sub-determinant integer programs.
notes: Stated as 'we do not know whether'; no labelled theorem environment.
